title: Tech at the Table: A Conversation with Premier Tony Wakeham
description: Andrea King speaks with Premier Tony Wakeham about the provincial economy and technology-sector growth.

summary.overview: In a conversation with techNL CEO Andrea King, Premier Tony Wakeham argued that government should make it easier for Newfoundland and Labrador technology companies to build, hire and sell—not simply add another layer of programmes and paperwork. The interview moved from economic-development support to private investment, provincial procurement, talent attraction, healthcare and artificial intelligence. Wakeham expressed support for reducing administrative friction and giving local innovators more opportunities to demonstrate solutions within the province. But several points were policy directions rather than detailed commitments: the discussion did not establish a new procurement rule, a funded AI strategy or a timetable for the proposed changes.

keyTakeaways.heading: Cutting red tape means changing how decisions move
keyTakeaways.explanation: Wakeham described the frustration of repeatedly completing forms and waiting while files pass between departments. He favoured a more streamlined, potentially one-stop approach and acknowledged that putting it in place would require significant work. He invited the technology community to identify specific barriers.

keyTakeaways.heading: Local firms need opportunities to prove their products at home
keyTakeaways.explanation: Discussing procurement, Wakeham said government purchasing should consider more than the lowest immediate price. He argued that business awarded locally can support employment, investment and tax revenue in the province. The conversation did not announce a procurement preference or provide implementation details.

keyTakeaways.heading: Technology growth is connected to wider provincial services
keyTakeaways.explanation: King raised healthcare access, skilled immigration and attracting families as essential factors in recruiting technology talent. Wakeham agreed those issues matter and linked growth to broader efforts on healthcare, workforce development and economic opportunity, including outside urban centres.

detailedSummary.heading: A broad promise of support, with specifics still to come
paragraphs: Wakeham opened by praising entrepreneurs and local firms creating jobs and attracting investment. He pointed to Newfoundland and Labrador companies competing in international markets as evidence that the province can produce successful technology businesses.

He described government’s role as creating conditions for investment, supporting commercialization, developing talent and reducing unnecessary barriers. Although the discussion touched on provincial budget support for innovation, the transcript does not clearly establish how much funding is newly available to technology firms, so no precise figure is presented here.

detailedSummary.heading: What simpler government processes might look like
paragraphs: Asked for a concrete example of making business easier, Wakeham focused on repetitive forms and proposals that circulate among multiple departments before an answer is issued. He said businesses should not have to navigate so many separate steps to get a decision.

He endorsed more coordinated access to government services and acknowledged that changes would not be effortless. The discussion offered a direction—simpler processes and faster responses—rather than a finished service model or rollout date.

detailedSummary.heading: Private investment and the government's purchasing power
paragraphs: King asked how the province might encourage more private money into local startups, mentioning possible investor incentives. Wakeham highlighted the importance of private-sector participation alongside public support and spoke favourably about leaving more resources with businesses and investors. He did not announce a specific new investor credit in the recorded exchange.

The conversation then turned to procurement. Wakeham argued that purchasing decisions should recognize the longer-term economic effects of supporting local firms, including jobs and taxes. He acknowledged procurement rules and tendering requirements; the interview did not establish that those rules had changed.

detailedSummary.heading: Attracting people means thinking beyond salaries
paragraphs: King connected technology-sector growth to the everyday considerations that influence whether skilled workers move to Newfoundland and Labrador: family services, access to a doctor, affordability and a welcoming community. She stressed the needs of newcomers who do not already have family or professional networks in the province.

Wakeham spoke about recruiting skilled workers, giving people opportunities to use their qualifications and improving access to healthcare. He also described how different parts of the province have different economic needs, suggesting that a single development strategy will not work equally well everywhere.

detailedSummary.heading: AI and rural development without one-size-fits-all plans
paragraphs: Asked whether government intended a broader artificial intelligence strategy, Wakeham said the province needed to listen to businesses and advisers about where AI could genuinely simplify work. He cautioned against producing a strategy merely for its own sake. The transcript does not contain a formal announcement of a new funded AI programme.

On rural development, Wakeham said government was speaking with communities about their distinct needs and opportunities. He emphasized the importance of connectivity and the possibility of building businesses beyond the province’s major urban centres.

notableIdeas: Wakeham repeatedly distinguished helping businesses from government making decisions for them.
The procurement exchange surfaced a tension between minimizing immediate purchase price and considering longer-term local economic benefits.
The interview contained supportive comments on AI adoption, but no specific governance, procurement or implementation plan was announced.
practicalApplications: For companies: document concrete examples of delays, repetitive forms or procurement barriers before raising them with techNL or government representatives.
For technology firms pursuing public-sector work: follow official procurement requirements as they stand; the Premier’s remarks were not a change in tendering rules.
For employers and policymakers: treat healthcare, credential recognition and rural connectivity as practical components of the technology talent strategy, not unrelated social issues.
